knowledge_statements.title: Distributed multifrontal solve
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Front owners assemble child updates, eliminate pivots upward through the tree, and solve by upward elimination followed by parallel downward back-substitution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(Ax=b\), a permutation \(P\), and distributed fronts indexed by an elimination tree, perform an upward pass. At each front \(\tau\), its owner assembles original matrix entries and update matrices received from children, factors the fully summed pivot block, stores its elimination factors, and sends the resulting Schur-complement update to the parent. At the root, factor the remaining block. Apply the stored factors to \(Pb\): traverse upward to eliminate pivot right-hand-side entries, solve the root system, then traverse downward to back-substitute independent child fronts in parallel. Return \(x=P^{\mathsf T}\widehat{x}\).
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is sparse, symmetric, and nonsingular under the selected pivoting policy.
Every matrix entry and child update has a unique destination front.
Dependencies imposed by the elimination tree are respected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: In exact arithmetic, the returned vector satisfies \(Ax=b\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elimination-tree multifrontal factorization and solve for a sparse symmetric linear system.

notation.meaning: A node, or front, of the elimination tree.

Those details are variant-dependent and require an exact multifrontal source locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel triangular solve
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unknowns on the same dependency level are computed concurrently; communication between levels supplies values needed by later substitutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a nonsingular lower-triangular matrix \(L\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) and distributed right-hand side \(b\), define the dependency graph with edge \(j\to i\) whenever \(j<i\) and \(L_{ij}\ne0\). Partition its vertices into levels \(\mathcal{L}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{L}_q\), so every predecessor of a vertex in \(\mathcal{L}_k\) lies in an earlier level. Initialize \(x=0\). For \(k=1,\ldots,q\), all owners concurrently compute \(x_i=(b_i-\sum_{j<i}L_{ij}x_j)/L_{ii}\) for local \(i\in\mathcal{L}_k\), then communicate newly required components before advancing. Return \(x\).
assumptions_latex: \(L_{ii}\ne0\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
The level partition is topologically valid for the nonzero dependency graph.
Communication completes before a dependent level begins.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After level \(\mathcal{L}_q\), the output satisfies \(Lx=b\) in exact arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Level-scheduled forward substitution for a distributed sparse lower-triangular system.

notation.meaning: Set of mutually independent row indices at dependency level \(k\).
Number of dependency levels, hence the number of sequential level stages.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Krylov KKT solve
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distributed right-preconditioned GMRES applies the KKT operator and preconditioner in parallel, uses global reductions for Arnoldi orthogonalization, returns immediately when the initial or a later iterate meets the residual tolerance, and explicitly reports nonconvergent Arnoldi breakdown or exhaustion of the iteration limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Kx=b\) be a distributed nonsingular KKT system, let \(M^{-1}\) be a fixed applicable right preconditioner, let \(0<\varepsilon<1\), and let \(j_{\max}\ge 1\) be an iteration limit. Choose \(x_0\), set \(r_0=b-Kx_0\), and set \(\beta=\lVert r_0\rVert_2\). If \(\beta\le\varepsilon\lVert b\rVert_2\), return \(x_0\). Otherwise set \(v_1=r_0/\beta\). At Arnoldi step \(j\), processes compute \(z_j=M^{-1}v_j\) and the distributed product \(w=Kz_j\); for \(i=1,\ldots,j\), they obtain \(h_{ij}=v_i^{\mathsf T}w\) by global reduction and update \(w\leftarrow w-h_{ij}v_i\). Set \(h_{j+1,j}=\lVert w\rVert_2\), form the Arnoldi matrix \(\overline H_j\), compute \(y_j\in\operatorname*{argmin}_y\lVert\beta e_1-\overline H_jy\rVert_2\), and set \(x_j=x_0+Z_jy_j\), where \(Z_j=[z_1,\ldots,z_j]\). If \(\lVert b-Kx_j\rVert_2\le\varepsilon\lVert b\rVert_2\), return \(x_j\). If \(h_{j+1,j}=0\) and the residual test fails, report Arnoldi breakdown; otherwise set \(v_{j+1}=w/h_{j+1,j}\) and continue. Report failure if no iterate passes the residual test by step \(j_{\max}\).
assumptions_latex: \(K\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is nonsingular, \(b\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\), and the distributed product by \(K\) is available.
\(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is fixed and nonsingular, and each application of \(M^{-1}\) is well defined.
\(0<\varepsilon<1\) and \(j_{\max}\in\mathbb{N}\) with \(j_{\max}\ge1\).
Exact residuals are evaluated at the declared stopping points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: On successful termination, the returned iterate \(x\) satisfies \(\lVert b-Kx\rVert_2\le\varepsilon\lVert b\rVert_2\); otherwise the algorithm reports Arnoldi breakdown or exhaustion of \(j_{\max}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Right-preconditioned distributed GMRES for a nonsingular KKT linear system, with initial-convergence and Arnoldi-breakdown handling.

notation.meaning: Upper-Hessenberg matrix produced by the first j Arnoldi steps.
First coordinate vector in the reduced least-squares space.
Maximum permitted number of Arnoldi steps.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical right-preconditioned distributed GMRES realization

knowledge_statements.title: Communication-avoiding Krylov solve
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method groups several Krylov products before a batched orthogonalization, reducing synchronization while retaining a block minimal-residual update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(Ax=b\), an initial vector \(x_0\), block length \(s\ge2\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon\), set \(r_0=b-Ax_0\). At outer iteration \(j\), generate the local polynomial block \(W_j=[r_j,Ar_j,\ldots,A^{s-1}r_j]\) using \(s-1\) successive distributed matrix-vector products without intervening inner-product reductions. Use one batched collective orthogonalization, such as block Gram computation followed by TSQR, to obtain a basis \(Q_j\) for \(\mathcal{K}_s(A,r_j)\). Compute \(z_j\in\operatorname*{argmin}_z\lVert r_j-AQ_jz\rVert_2\), set \(x_{j+1}=x_j+Q_jz_j\), and recompute \(r_{j+1}\). Stop when \(\lVert r_{j+1}\rVert_2\le\varepsilon\lVert b\rVert_2\), or report the iteration limit.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), \(b\ne0\), \(s\ge2\), and \(0<\varepsilon<1\).
Each generated block has the rank required to represent \(\mathcal{K}_s(A,r_j)\), or rank deficiency is detected.
Distributed products by \(A\) and stable batched orthogonalization are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accepted update minimizes the residual over \(x_j+\mathcal{K}_s(A,r_j)\), and successful termination satisfies the prescribed relative-residual test.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An s-step minimal-residual Krylov method with batched orthogonalization.

notation.meaning: Number of Krylov powers grouped between synchronization stages.
Polynomial Krylov block generated at outer iteration \(j\).
Orthonormal basis for the current block Krylov subspace.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The record describes a plausible restarted s-step minimal-residual construction and algorithm is the correct content kind, but no source supports the precise polynomial basis, rank handling, batched orthogonalization, or the assertion about synchronization. In particular, the communication behavior of the proposed Gram/TSQR realization is implementation-dependent and needs an exact communication-avoiding Krylov locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed preconditioner application
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Processes restrict the residual, solve subdomain systems concurrently, and sum overlapping corrections to apply an additive Schwarz preconditioner.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let overlapping subdomains have restriction matrices \(R_i\) and nonsingular local matrices \(B_i\). For a distributed residual \(r\), define the additive Schwarz operator \(M^{-1}=\sum_{i=1}^{p}R_i^{\mathsf T}B_i^{-1}R_i\). Each process owning subdomain \(i\) gathers the halo entries needed for \(r_i=R_ir\), computes \(B_i z_i=r_i\) exactly or to a declared local tolerance, and scatters \(R_i^{\mathsf T}z_i\) to the owners of global indices. Owners sum all overlapping contributions and return \(z=\sum_{i=1}^{p}R_i^{\mathsf T}z_i\). A failure is reported if a local solve fails its declared tolerance.
assumptions_latex: Each \(B_i\) is nonsingular.
The restrictions \(R_i\) cover every global degree of freedom requiring a correction.
Overlapping contributions are combined by an exact distributed sum in the stated arithmetic model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: With exact local solves, the returned vector equals \(z=M^{-1}r\); with inexact solves, it is the declared inexact preconditioner application.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributed additive Schwarz application with parallel local subdomain solves.

notation.meaning: Restriction from global coordinates to subdomain \(i\).

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical distributed additive Schwarz application

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The exact-solve branch correctly realizes the stated additive Schwarz operator and an algorithmic application fits the computational-mechanism leaf. No citation supports the selected additive Schwarz variant, however, and the meaning of the inexact application depends on the local stopping policy; an authoritative domain-decomposition locator is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Benders subproblem solve
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Workers solve independent scenario recourse problems, return Benders optimality or feasibility cuts, and the coordinator adds all cuts before resolving the master.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a master iterate \(x^k\), dispatch every scenario \(s\in S\) to a worker. The worker solves \[Q_s(x^k)=\min_{y_s\ge 0}\{q_s^{\mathsf T}y_s:W_sy_s=h_s-T_sx^k\}.\] If the problem is feasible and bounded, it returns an optimal dual vector \(\pi_s^k\) and the cut \(\theta_s\ge (\pi_s^k)^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx)\), where \(W_s^{\mathsf T}\pi_s^k\le q_s\). If it is infeasible, it returns a dual ray \(r_s^k\) satisfying \(W_s^{\mathsf T}r_s^k\le0\) and the feasibility cut \((r_s^k)^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx)\le0\). After all workers finish, add every returned cut, resolve the master, and stop when no violated feasibility cut remains and every recourse gap is within tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is finite and each scenario recourse problem is a linear program.
The current master solution \(x^k\) is available identically to all workers.
Each worker returns either a valid optimal dual solution or a valid infeasibility ray.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every returned inequality is valid for the corresponding scenario recourse epigraph or feasibility domain, and the cuts may be generated concurrently.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Synchronous multi-cut Benders execution for a finite-scenario two-stage linear program.

notation.meaning: optimal dual vector and infeasibility ray

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits this computational-mechanism leaf, but the exact Benders formulation has no citation. The infeasibility certificate should explicitly require positive violation at the current iterate, \((r_s^k)^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx^k)>0\), in addition to \(W_s^{\mathsf T}r_s^k\le0\). The phrase “every recourse gap” is undefined and needs a sourced, precisely specified stopping test.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel scenario decomposition
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scenario workers solve proximal local problems in parallel; the coordinator averages their decisions and updates consensus multipliers until primal and dual residuals are small.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\sum_{s\in S}p_sf_s(x_s)\) subject to \(x_s=z\) for all \(s\in S\), where \(p_s>0\) and \(\sum_sp_s=1\). Initialize \(z^0\), scaled multipliers \(u_s^0\), and \(\rho>0\). At iteration \(k\), solve concurrently \[x_s^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X_s}\left(f_s(x)+\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert x-z^k+u_s^k\rVert^2\right).\] After collecting the scenario solutions, set \[z^{k+1}=\sum_{s\in S}p_s(x_s^{k+1}+u_s^k),\qquad u_s^{k+1}=u_s^k+x_s^{k+1}-z^{k+1}.\] Stop when the primal consensus residuals and the change in \(z\) satisfy prescribed tolerances; output \(z^{k+1}\).
assumptions_latex: Each \(X_s\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and each \(f_s\) is proper, closed, and convex.
The consensus problem has a solution and an applicable saddle point.
Every iteration collects one completed update from every scenario.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed worker solves are mutually independent conditional on \((z^k,u_s^k)\), so the scenario step is executable in parallel.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consensus ADMM execution for finite convex scenario subproblems with a shared decision.

notation.meaning: scenario decision and shared consensus decision

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind and synchronous parallel-worker interpretation fit the leaf. However, no source supports this particular probability-weighted consensus ADMM variant. Because the objective contains \(p_sf_s\), while the local objective omits \(p_s\) and the coordinator uses a weighted average, a source must establish the intended weighted augmented-Lagrangian scaling and corresponding residual test.

knowledge_statements.title: Asynchronous decomposition worker
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Workers evaluate decomposition oracles on possibly stale tagged states; the coordinator incorporates admissible messages immediately and rejects updates exceeding a fixed delay bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a coordinator maintain states \(v^0,v^1,\ldots\) and let worker \(i\) implement a decomposition oracle \(\mathcal O_i\). Worker \(i\) reads a tagged state \((v^{\tau},\tau)\), computes \(m_i=\mathcal O_i(v^{\tau})\), and returns \((i,m_i,\tau)\) without waiting for other workers. Upon the \(k\)-th accepted arrival, the coordinator accepts the message only if \(0\le k-\tau\le D\), then performs \[v^{k+1}=\mathcal U(v^k;i,m_i,\tau).\] A message with \(k-\tau>D\) is discarded or assigned a fresh state. Workers immediately request another state. Stop when a coordinator-defined residual \(R(v^k)\) is at most \(\varepsilon\); output \(v^k\).
assumptions_latex: The delay bound satisfies \(D\in\mathbb N\).
Every worker message identifies its worker and the state version used to compute it.
The update map \(\mathcal U\) preserves the coordinator's required feasibility or validity invariants.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Accepted worker messages require no iteration-wide synchronization and have staleness at most \(D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Version-tagged server-worker execution with bounded-staleness admission and no global barrier.

notation.meaning: coordinator state after k accepted messages
decomposition oracle executed by worker i

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel pricing problem solve
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Block workers independently minimize reduced cost under common master dual prices; all improving columns are added together before the restricted master is resolved.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let block \(i\) have columns \((a_{ip},c_{ip})\) indexed by \(p\in P_i\). Solve the restricted master and broadcast its coupling dual vector \(\pi^k\) and convexity dual values \(\sigma_i^k\). Concurrently, each worker computes \[p_i^k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{p\in P_i}\left(c_{ip}-(\pi^k)^{\mathsf T}a_{ip}-\sigma_i^k\right)\] and returns the minimizing column and reduced cost \(\bar c_i^k\). Add every returned column satisfying \(\bar c_i^k< -\varepsilon\), then resolve the restricted master. If all workers report \(\bar c_i^k\ge -\varepsilon\), stop and output its current solution; for \(\varepsilon=0\), absence of negative-reduced-cost columns is the pricing termination condition for the full master linear program.
assumptions_latex: The full master is a linear Dantzig–Wolfe formulation with block column sets \(P_i\).
The restricted master is feasible and solved to dual optimality at each pricing round.
Each worker solves its pricing problem globally over \(P_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pricing problems are conditionally independent given \((\pi^k,\sigma^k)\), and \(\bar c_i^k\ge0\) for every block certifies that no omitted column improves the linear master.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parallel block pricing for a Dantzig–Wolfe restricted master linear program.

notation.meaning: column index set for block i
minimum reduced cost in block i

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits this column-generation execution leaf, and the conditional independence of block pricing problems is correctly scoped. No citation is supplied for the reduced-cost formula or the claim that nonnegative minimum reduced cost in every block certifies the full master LP termination condition; that claim requires a source specifying the Dantzig–Wolfe master conventions and dual signs.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel cut separation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Workers search distinct cut families for inequalities violated by the same relaxation point; the coordinator adds their union and stops when all searches find none.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a relaxation contain a base set \(P_0\) and cut families \(a_{ij}^{\mathsf T}x\le b_{ij}\), with \(j\in J_i\) assigned to worker \(i\). After solving the current relaxation, broadcast \(\bar x^k\). Each worker independently computes \[j_i^k\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{j\in J_i}\left(a_{ij}^{\mathsf T}\bar x^k-b_{ij}\right)\] or invokes an equivalent exact separation oracle. It returns a cut when its maximum violation exceeds \(\varepsilon\). The coordinator removes duplicate inequalities, adds the union of returned cuts, and resolves. Stop when every worker reports maximum violation at most \(\varepsilon\); output \(\bar x^k\). For \(\varepsilon=0\), termination certifies membership in every represented cut family.
assumptions_latex: Every inequality \(a_{ij}^{\mathsf T}x\le b_{ij}\) is valid for the target feasible set.
The worker families jointly cover all cut families represented by the procedure.
Each worker performs exact separation, or reports a valid certified upper bound on maximum violation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: All returned inequalities may be separated concurrently, and zero-tolerance termination implies \(a_{ij}^{\mathsf T}\bar x^k\le b_{ij}\) for every represented pair \((i,j)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Synchronous parallel separation over partitioned families of valid linear inequalities.

notation.meaning: cut indices assigned to worker i

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the parallel cut-separation leaf, and the zero-tolerance conclusion is appropriately restricted to the represented cut families under exact separation. No source is supplied for the synchronous separation procedure or its termination certificate. A cited treatment should also clarify existence of the displayed argmax when a family \(J_i\) is infinite, or formulate the step solely through an exact separation oracle.

children.title: Distributed Solver Scheduling, Load Balancing, and Communication

knowledge_statements.title: Solver task queue
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Source tasks initially enter a precedence-aware FIFO queue. An idle worker atomically moves the first queued task into the running set. Successful completion releases previously unqueued successors whose predecessors are complete, while failure returns the task to the queue. The procedure stops exactly when every task is complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite directed acyclic task graph, where \((u,v)\in E\) means that task \(v\) requires the output of task \(u\). Let \(Q\) be an ordered queue, \(R\subseteq V\) the set of running tasks, and \(C\subseteq V\) the set of successfully completed tasks. Initialize \(R=C=\varnothing\) and initialize \(Q\) with all tasks \(v\in V\) satisfying \(\operatorname{pred}(v)=\varnothing\), ordered by a fixed tie-breaking key. Whenever a worker becomes idle and \(Q\) is nonempty, atomically remove the first task \(u\) from \(Q\), add \(u\) to \(R\), and assign it to that worker. If \(u\) succeeds, atomically remove it from \(R\), add it to \(C\), and enqueue, in tie-breaking order, every task \(v\in V\setminus(C\cup R\cup\operatorname{elts}(Q))\) satisfying \(\operatorname{pred}(v)\subseteq C\). If \(u\) fails, atomically remove it from \(R\) and append it to \(Q\) without adding it to \(C\). Stop and return the task outputs exactly when \(C=V\).
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed acyclic graph.
Queue, running-set, and completed-set transitions are atomic.
Every running task eventually reports either success or failure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every task moved from \(Q\) to \(R\) has all predecessors in \(C\), no task occupies two execution states simultaneously, and the procedure stops exactly when \(C=V\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A precedence-aware FIFO queue for dispatching finite solver tasks to distributed workers.

notation.meaning: set of immediate predecessors of task v
set of tasks currently contained in queue Q

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic load balancing
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each balancing epoch, examine the finite set of feasible migrations between distinct workers. Migrate the candidate with the smallest communication-aware predicted maximum load only if it improves the current predicted maximum by at least the prescribed threshold; perform no migration when no qualifying candidate exists.

At a balancing epoch, let \(I=\{1,\ldots,p\}\) with \(p\geq2\) be the worker set. For each \(i\in I\), let \(Q_i\) be its finite set of movable tasks and let \(\ell_i\geq0\) be its predicted remaining processing load. For each ordered pair \(i,j\in I\) with \(i
e j\), let \(\mathcal F_{ij}\) be a finite collection of nonempty feasible subsets of \(Q_i\). For every \(S\in\mathcal F_{ij}\), compute \[M(i,j,S)=\max\!\left(\{\ell_i-w(S),\,\ell_j+w(S)+c_{ij}(S)\}\cup\{\ell_k:k\in I\setminus\{i,j\}\}ight).\] Let \(\mathcal A=\{(i,j,S):i,j\in I,\ i
e j,\ S\in\mathcal F_{ij}\}\). If \(\mathcal A
e\varnothing\), choose \((i^*,j^*,S^*)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{(i,j,S)\in\mathcal A}M(i,j,S)\). If \(M(i^*,j^*,S^*)\leq\max_{k\in I}\ell_k-\delta\), atomically migrate \(S^*\) from \(i^*\) to \(j^*\); otherwise perform no migration. If \(\mathcal A=\varnothing\), perform no migration. Re-estimate affected loads after each completion or migration and apply the rule again at the next balancing epoch.

For every candidate \(S\in\mathcal F_{ij}\), the estimates satisfy \(0<w(S)\leq\ell_i\) and \(c_{ij}(S)\geq0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Granularity control for solver tasks
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose task size by minimizing a measured makespan model that accounts for worker parallelism, processing rate, per-task overhead, and communication cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(W>0\) homogeneous work units remain for \(p\geq1\) workers. Let \(G\) be a finite set of admissible task sizes. For each \(g\in G\), form \(N(g)=\lceil W/g\rceil\) tasks, with the final task containing any remainder, and predict \[\widehat T(g)=\left\lceil\frac{N(g)}{p}\right\rceil\left(\frac{g}{r}+oight)+c(g),\] where \(r\) is the measured processing rate, \(o\) is per-task scheduling overhead, and \(c(g)\) estimates communication cost. Choose \(g^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{g\in G}\widehat T(g)\), partition the remaining work accordingly, and recompute \(g^*\) whenever updated measurements change the predicted minimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(W>0\), \(p\geq1\), and \(G\) is finite and nonempty.
The measured rate satisfies \(r>0\), while \(o\geq0\) and \(c(g)\geq0\).
Work units may be partitioned at every size \(g\in G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected granularity satisfies \(\widehat T(g^*)=\min_{g\in G}\widehat T(g)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A model-based rule balancing parallel slack against per-task scheduling and communication overhead.

knowledge_statements.title: Barrier synchronization in parallel solves
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A barrier prevents every worker from passing into the next superstep until all participants have arrived. Its release time is no earlier than the last arrival, and each early worker waits until release; in an ideal zero-overhead model, release occurs at the last-arrival time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(p\geq1\) workers executing supersteps \(k=0,1,\ldots\). Let \(a_i^k\) be the time at which worker \(i\) reaches the barrier ending superstep \(k\), and define the last-arrival time by \[b^k=\max_{1\leq j\leq p}a_j^k.\] A barrier synchronization prevents every worker from passing the barrier and beginning superstep \(k+1\) before all participating workers have arrived. If \(r^k\) is the logical release time, then \(r^k\geq b^k\). Writing \(\lambda^k=r^k-b^k\geq0\) for barrier-release latency, worker \(i\) waits \(w_i^k=r^k-a_i^k\). In the ideal zero-overhead barrier model, \(\lambda^k=0\) and hence \(r^k=b^k\).
assumptions_latex: The participant set \(\{1,ldots,p\}\) is fixed during each barrier instance.
Every participating worker eventually reaches the barrier.
Barrier arrivals and the logical release event are reliably recorded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every worker \(i\), passage into superstep \(k+1\) occurs no earlier than \(r^k\geq b^k=\max_j a_j^k\), and its barrier waiting time is \(w_i^k=r^k-a_i^k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bulk-synchronous barrier semantics for one parallel solver superstep, including possible barrier-release latency.

notation.meaning: time at which worker i reaches the barrier after superstep k
last-arrival time for the barrier instance
latency between the last arrival and barrier release

knowledge_statements.title: Asynchronous solver communication
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Workers send versioned states without blocking, retain each neighbor's newest received state, and update from local caches without waiting at a global barrier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Worker \(i\) stores local state \(x_i\), local version \(v_i\), and the newest received pair \((v_j,x_j)\) for each required neighbor \(j\). After any local update, it increments \(v_i\) and sends \((i,v_i,x_i)\) without waiting for acknowledgments or other workers. Upon receiving \((j,v,x)\), it replaces the cached pair for \(j\) exactly when \(v\) exceeds the cached version. Whenever locally activated, worker \(i\) computes its next solver update from its current state and cached neighbor states. Execution uses no global barrier and stops only when a distributed termination certificate is obtained; otherwise it produces an asynchronous state sequence indefinitely.
assumptions_latex: Messages are not corrupted and versions from each sender are totally ordered.
Each worker is activated infinitely often unless termination is certified.
Every sent message is eventually delivered, although delays may vary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each cache version is nondecreasing, and no local update requires simultaneous readiness of all workers.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Versioned nonblocking communication using locally cached solver states and no global barrier.

notation.meaning: current solver state at worker i
newest cached version and state received from neighbor j

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits asynchronous solver communication, and cache-version monotonicity follows from the stated replacement rule. However, the cited general communication and asynchronous-algorithm sections have not been shown to support this exact versioned-cache protocol or its distributed termination-certificate requirement. The worker set, neighbor sets, state spaces, initial cache versions, and certificate semantics are also undefined. Full-text evidence for the protocol, or a more specific authoritative source and locator, is required before choosing a reliable mathematical revision.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let clients \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) retain local data governed by distributions \(\mathcal D_i\). Let \(f_i(w)=\mathbb E_{\xi\sim\mathcal D_i}[\ell_i(w;\xi)]\) and let weights \(p_i\ge0\) satisfy \(\sum_i p_i=1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinator-mediated optimization of a shared finite-dimensional model under persistent data locality, heterogeneous clients, and possibly partial participation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Federated optimization is the problem \(\min_{w\in W}F(w)=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i f_i(w)\), or its population-client analogue, under the information constraint that raw client data remain local and the optimization protocol exchanges model states, updates, statistics, or protected messages rather than pooling the underlying samples. At communication round \(t\), only a subset \(S_t\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) may participate; participating clients may perform multiple local computations before transmitting, and a coordinator combines the returned information. The mathematical objective and the communication-participation process are both part of the problem specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Federated optimization minimizes a weighted aggregate of client risks while client data remain at their sources. Clients compute from local data and communicate permitted updates or statistics, typically through a coordinator. Participation can vary by round, and clients may perform several local computations between communication events. The definition requires both a global objective and an information pattern; merely partitioning an ordinary centralized dataset does not by itself specify a federated deployment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The canonical shared-model objective is \(\min_{w\in W}\sum_i p_i\mathbb E_{\xi\sim\mathcal D_i}[\ell_i(w;\xi)]\) subject to local data access and protocol-defined communication.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For finite local datasets \(D_i\), one may take \(f_i(w)=|D_i|^{-1}\sum_{\xi\in D_i}\ell_i(w;\xi)\).
special_cases_latex: Choosing \(p_i=|D_i|/\sum_j|D_j|\) yields the empirical risk over the union of disjoint local samples without physically pooling them.
Full participation has \(S_t=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) at every round.
immediate_consequences_latex: Nonidentical \(\mathcal D_i\) generally produce distinct local objectives even though all clients optimize a shared parameter.
boundary_notes: Data locality alone does not guarantee privacy, security, or robustness.
Personalized and model-heterogeneous federation require objectives with client-specific parameters.

children.title: Federated Optimization Settings
children.top_down_role: Deployment and objective regimes distinguished by population scale, data alignment, and coordination.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal I\) be a finite or measurable client population, let \(P\) be a probability law on clients, and for each client \(i\) let \(\mathcal D_i\) be a local data law and \(f_i:W\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) its local objective.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shared-model federated objectives covering finite-client and population-client formulations; topology and algorithm are specified separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A federated optimization problem is the tuple \((W,\mathcal I,P,\{\mathcal D_i,f_i\}_{i\in\mathcal I},\mathfrak A)\), where \(W\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is the parameter domain and \(\mathfrak A\) is an admissible information-access and coordination model, with objective \(\min_{w\in W}F(w)=\mathbb E_{i\sim P}[f_i(w)]\). In the finite case, \(P(i)=p_i\) and \(F(w)=\sum_i p_i f_i(w)\). The access model requires evaluation or estimation of \(f_i\) to occur at client \(i\) and specifies which clients may be queried and which messages may be communicated. A solution is any \(w_\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{w\in W}F(w)\), when the argmin is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A federated optimization problem specifies a parameter domain, a client population and its weighting law, each client's local data and objective, and the permitted access and coordination pattern. Its global objective is the expectation of the local objective over clients. For finitely many clients this is a weighted sum. The formal problem therefore distinguishes what is optimized from how local information may be accessed; an algorithm is not part of the solution definition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w_\star\) solves the problem exactly when \(w_\star\in W\) and \(F(w_\star)=\inf_{w\in W}\mathbb E_{i\sim P}[f_i(w)]\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The finite-population form is recovered by the discrete law \(P=\sum_i p_i\delta_i\).
special_cases_latex: Uniform client weighting uses \(p_i=1/n\); sample weighting uses weights proportional to local dataset sizes.
immediate_consequences_latex: Changing \(P\) changes the optimization problem even if every local objective is unchanged.
boundary_notes: The definition does not require convexity or differentiability.
A deployment label such as cross-device or cross-silo adds population and availability assumptions, not a different algebraic minimizer definition by itself.

notation.meaning: client weighting or sampling law defining the target objective

review_flags: No inspected authoritative source supports the complete tuple-based problem specification.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Device Federated Optimization

Cross-device federated optimization minimizes
\[F(w)=\sum_{i=1}^m p_iF_i(w),\qquad F_i(w)=\mathbb E_{\xi\sim P_i}[\ell(w;\xi)],\]
over a shared parameter \(w\in\mathbb R^d\), where the client population is large and each communication round accesses only an available subset \(S_t\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Client data remain local, participation may be intermittent, and the server update is computed from messages produced by clients in \(S_t\), rather than from simultaneous access to all local objectives or datasets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A large population of intermittently available devices jointly minimizes a weighted objective through sampled client participation while retaining data locally.
assumptions_latex: All clients optimize a common parameter space \(\mathbb R^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cross-device regime is characterized by the weighted federated objective and partial, availability-dependent client participation.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Cross-device federated optimization is the population objective \(\min_{w\in W}F(w)=\mathbb E_{i\sim P}[f_i(w)]\) under the regime in which \(\mathcal I\) is large, an individual device need not be continuously addressable, and each round uses a finite selected subset \(S_t\subseteq A_t\subseteq\mathcal I\). Device \(i\) can evaluate its local objective only while available, raw data remain on that device, and the protocol must define selection probabilities \(q_{i,t}=\Pr(i\in S_t\mid i\in A_t,\mathcal H_t)\) or an equivalent sampling rule. Resource restrictions limit local computation, storage, energy, or communication per participation event.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cross-device federated optimization targets the client-population risk across many end-user devices. Devices are intermittently available and only a finite subset participates in any round. Local data remain on devices, while the protocol communicates permitted updates. A complete mathematical specification includes the target client distribution and the availability and selection process, because observed participants may not represent the target population.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The target remains \(\min_w\mathbb E_{i\sim P}[f_i(w)]\), while admissible observations at round \(t\) are restricted to the selected available set \(S_t\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a finite but very large device population, \(P\) may be a discrete distribution and the expectation becomes a weighted sum.
special_cases_latex: Uniform sampling from currently available devices has \(q_{i,t}=m_t/|A_t|\) when exactly \(m_t\) devices are selected.
immediate_consequences_latex: Availability-biased selection can target an objective different from the intended law \(P\) unless corrected.

unreliable edge-client participation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Edge-client participation is unreliable when at least one repeatedly eligible device has a nontrivial conditional probability of becoming unavailable before its round response is delivered.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For device set \([N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}\), let \(A_{i,t}\in\{0,1\}\) indicate that device \(i\), if invited in round \(t\), remains available through the response deadline. Participation is unreliable when some recurrent device has genuinely random availability: there exist \(i\) and infinitely many rounds \(t\) for which \(0<\mathbb{P}(A_{i,t}=1\mid\mathcal H_t)<1\). Any realized responding set \(S_t\) must then satisfy \(S_t\subseteq\{i:A_{i,t}=1\}\); no fixed client set is guaranteed to respond in every round.

\(\mathcal H_t\) contains all information revealed before round-\(t\) availability is realized.

knowledge_statements.title: large-client-population regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deployment is in the large-client-population regime when the eligible population grows while each round samples an asymptotically vanishing fraction of it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a sequence of federated systems indexed by the eligible population size \(N\to\infty\). If \(S_{N,t}\subseteq[N]\) is the set participating in round \(t\), define the conditional participation fraction by \(q_{N,t}=\mathbb{E}[|S_{N,t}|\mid\mathcal H_{N,t}]/N\). The sequence is in the large-client-population regime when, for every fixed round \(t\), \(q_{N,t}\to0\). Thus the server interacts with an asymptotically negligible fraction of the eligible population in each fixed round, even if the cohort size grows.
assumptions_latex: The systems have eligible populations \([N]\) with \(N\to\infty\).
The conditional expected cohort size \(\mathbb{E}[|S_{N,t}|\mid\mathcal H_{N,t}]\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\forall t\text{ fixed},\qquad \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{\mathbb{E}[|S_{N,t}|\mid\mathcal H_{N,t}]}{N}=0.\]

knowledge_statements.title: high-availability client assumption
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every persistent silo remains available through each round with conditional probability at least a prescribed high threshold; perfect availability is the threshold-one special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_{k,t}\in\{0,1\}\) indicate that organizational client \(k\) is available for the entirety of round \(t\), and let \(\mathcal H_t\) be the pre-round history. For a prescribed \(\delta\in[0,1)\), the high-availability assumption holds when \(\mathbb{P}(A_{k,t}=1\mid\mathcal H_t)\geq1-\delta\) almost surely for every client and round. The full-participation availability idealization is the special case \(\delta=0\); availability alone does not require the server to select every available client.
assumptions_latex: The client set \([K]\) is persistent across rounds.
Availability is measured from round invitation through the response deadline.
\(\delta\in[0,1)\) is fixed independently of the client and round.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\inf_{k\in[K],\,t\geq0}\mathbb{P}(A_{k,t}=1\mid\mathcal H_t)\geq1-\delta\quad\text{almost surely}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform conditional availability condition for persistent cross-silo clients.

notation.meaning: Round-long availability indicator for silo k.

The intended cross-silo assumption may instead be deterministic availability, frequent participation, or bounded dropout.

children.title: Federated Data Partitioning
children.top_down_role: Federation distinguished by sample, feature, and task alignment.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For client \(i\), let \(R_i\) be its entity or sample identifiers, \(C_i\) its observed feature coordinates, and \(T_i\) its prediction-task or label coordinates.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A set-theoretic taxonomy of federations by alignment of entities, features, and tasks; privacy-preserving record linkage is outside the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The alignment signature of a federation is the pattern of overlap among \(\{R_i\}\), \(\{C_i\}\), and \(\{T_i\}\). A federation is horizontally aligned when clients share a common feature and task space, \(C_i=C\) and \(T_i=T\), while their entity sets are principally disjoint or only weakly overlapping. It is vertically aligned when participating clients refer to a materially overlapping entity set but hold distinct feature blocks, so \(R_i\approx R\) and the \(C_i\) are complementary. It is transfer or task-heterogeneous when both entity and feature overlap are limited or when task spaces differ, requiring an explicit relation among client representations or tasks. The symbols indicating approximate overlap must be replaced in an application by declared overlap thresholds or linkage relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The federation alignment taxonomy classifies clients according to which entities, feature coordinates, and tasks they share. Horizontal federation uses a common feature and task space across mostly different entities. Vertical federation uses overlapping entities whose attributes are split across clients. Transfer or task-heterogeneous federation has limited alignment or distinct tasks and therefore needs an explicit relation connecting representations or objectives. Any use of approximate overlap requires an application-specific threshold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Classification is determined by the overlap signature \((\{R_i\},\{C_i\},\{T_i\})\), not merely by the number or type of clients.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Horizontal alignment is often called sample-partitioned federation, while vertical alignment is often called feature-partitioned federation.
special_cases_latex: If all clients have identical \(C_i\) and \(T_i\) and pairwise disjoint \(R_i\), the federation is purely horizontal.
If all clients share the same linked entities and the feature blocks partition \(C\), the federation is purely vertical.
immediate_consequences_latex: Vertical federation requires entity alignment before losses involving joined feature vectors can be evaluated.
boundary_notes: Real deployments may be hybrid and need not belong uniquely to one class.
Feature alignment is distinct from equality of feature distributions.

notation.meaning: entity, feature-coordinate, and task-coordinate sets of client i

review_flags: No inspected source supports the precise taxonomy and overlap conventions.
knowledge_statements.title: Sample-feature-task alignment taxonomy
Horizontal Federation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clients share the same feature and label schema but hold different observational units, so training aggregates objectives across row-partitioned data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A federation is horizontal when every client records the same feature-label schema \(\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\), while clients hold distinct observational units. Formally, client \(i\) owns
\[D_i=\{(x_{ik},y_{ik}):k\in I_i\}\subseteq\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y,\]
with aligned coordinates across clients and typically disjoint identifier sets \(I_i\cap I_j=\varnothing\) for \(i\ne j\). Training minimizes an aggregate such as \(F(w)=\sum_i p_i|I_i|^{-1}\sum_{k\in I_i}\ell(w;x_{ik},y_{ik})\) without transferring the records in \(D_i\).
assumptions_latex: All clients use a common feature space \(\mathcal X\), label space \(\mathcal Y\), and model parameter \(w\).
Client record identifiers are aligned sufficiently to determine whether units overlap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Horizontal federation represents a row-wise partition of a common-schema learning dataset.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Federation aligned by feature schema but partitioned by observational units.

notation.meaning: record identifiers held by client i

review_flags: No supplied locator supports the horizontal-federation taxonomy.
standard_field_rationale: common features with differing sample identities is the conventional horizontal partition.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits this taxonomy leaf and the row-partition interpretation is standard, but no authoritative citation with a specific locator supports the exact definition, including the typical disjointness condition.

knowledge_statements.title: Vertical Federation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clients share entity identities but hold different feature columns, jointly evaluating a model whose loss depends on the combined feature blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A federation is vertical when clients describe overlapping entities but hold different feature blocks. For a shared identifier set \(I\), client \(i\) holds \(x_k^{(i)}\in\mathcal X_i\) for entity \(k\in I\), and the complete covariate is
\[x_k=(x_k^{(1)},\ldots,x_k^{(m)})\in\mathcal X_1\times\cdots\times\mathcal X_m.\]
Labels may be held by one designated client. The parties jointly minimize a loss depending on the combined feature blocks while neither raw block nor entity-level records are centrally pooled.
assumptions_latex: A privacy-preserving entity-alignment procedure identifies the common set \(I\).
Feature blocks have a specified common model and loss.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Vertical federation represents a column-wise feature partition over aligned entities.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Federation aligned by entities but partitioned by feature coordinates.

notation.meaning: features of entity k held by client i

review_flags: No supplied locator supports the vertical-federation taxonomy.
standard_field_rationale: shared entities with differing feature blocks is the conventional vertical partition.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits this taxonomy leaf and the feature-partition interpretation is standard, but no authoritative citation with a specific locator supports the stated entity-alignment and label-placement formulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Transfer Federation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clients with mismatched samples and feature spaces collaborate through a shared representation or transfer term rather than direct row or column alignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A federation is a transfer federation when participating clients have limited overlap in both observational units and feature spaces, so neither a common-schema horizontal partition nor an entity-aligned vertical partition applies. Client \(i\) has data from \(P_i\) on \(\mathcal X_i\times\mathcal Y_i\), and collaboration uses learned maps \(T_i:\mathcal X_i\to\mathcal Z\) or shared parameters to transfer information through a common representation space \(\mathcal Z\). The optimized objective couples client-specific prediction losses with an explicit cross-domain transfer or representation-alignment term.
assumptions_latex: At least two clients lack both complete entity alignment and a common feature schema.
A specified transfer map, shared representation, or cross-domain coupling relates their learning tasks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Transfer federation couples otherwise nonaligned client domains through an explicit transferable representation or parameter relation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Federation requiring transfer across mismatched sample and feature domains.

notation.meaning: client-specific map into a shared representation

review_flags: Transfer-federation definitions vary, and no directly supporting locator was supplied.
The exact required transfer mechanism needs authoritative source confirmation.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the taxonomy leaf, but transfer-federation terminology is not uniform. No source supports the asserted requirement of learned maps, shared representations, or an explicit alignment term, so the mathematical scope cannot be validated reliably.

children.title: Decentralized Federated Optimization
children.top_down_role: Federated objectives optimized without a permanent central aggregator.

knowledge_statements.title: Decentralized Federated Optimization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clients optimize local objectives and enforce model consensus through peer-to-peer communication on a connected graph, without a permanent central aggregator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected client communication graph. Decentralized federated optimization solves
\[\min_{w_1,\ldots,w_m}\ \sum_{i=1}^m p_iF_i(w_i)\quad\text{subject to}\quad w_i=w_j\ \text{for every }\{i,j\}\in E,\]
where client \(i\) evaluates \(F_i\) from its local data and exchanges model-derived messages only with graph neighbors. No permanent central aggregator computes the global update. Connectivity makes edge consensus equivalent to a common model \(w_1=\cdots=w_m\), recovering the weighted federated objective.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is connected and undirected.
\(p_i\ge0\) and \(\sum_i p_i=1\).
Each \(F_i\) is defined on a common parameter space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible points satisfy \(w_1=\cdots=w_m\), reducing the problem to \(\min_w\sum_i p_iF_i(w)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consensus formulation of a federated objective without a permanent central server.
review_flags: The source supports graph-consensus optimization; federated terminology remains to be checked.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The graph-consensus formulation is mathematically coherent and the definition role fits the leaf. However, the cited section supports decentralized graph-consensus optimization rather than the stronger federated characterization involving local data and absence of a permanent aggregator. A federated-optimization source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Federated Coordinator Architectures
children.top_down_role: Coordinator-mediated optimization with persistent data locality and heterogeneous participation.

knowledge_statements.title: Federated Coordination Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coordinator optimizes a weighted client objective using messages from varying participant subsets, while each client's samples remain local.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The federated coordination boundary for \(\min_x F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n p_iF_i(x)\), where \(p_i\geq0\) and \(\sum_i p_i=1\), is the interface under which a coordinator broadcasts \(x^t\) and participating client \(i\in S_t\) returns \(M_i^t=\Phi_i(x^t;P_i,\xi_i^t)\). The coordinator updates \(x^{t+1}=\Psi_t(x^t,\{M_i^t:i\in S_t\})\). Persistent data locality means that samples from \(P_i\) remain at client \(i\); heterogeneous participation permits \(S_t\) and the local maps \(\Phi_i\) to vary across clients and rounds.
assumptions_latex: Client \(i\) holds a local objective \(F_i(x)=\mathbb{E}_{\zeta\sim P_i}[\ell(x;\zeta)]\).
At round \(t\), only clients in \(S_t\) participate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coordinator observes \(\{M_i^t:i\in S_t\}\), but neither \(P_i\) nor the underlying samples.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinator-mediated finite-client model with persistent data locality and partial participation.

notation.meaning: Client participation set at round t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard coordinator-mediated federated optimization model

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The definition matches the federated-coordination leaf and distinguishes local data from disclosed messages, but no citation is supplied for the weighted client objective, partial participation, persistent data locality, or heterogeneous local maps. Standard-field rationale alone is insufficient for this nontrivial candidate.

children.title: Federated Optimization Assumptions and Heterogeneity
children.top_down_role: Client differences and participation processes that shape federated optimization.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For clients \(i\in\mathcal I\), let \(f_i\) be local objectives, \(M_i\) local model spaces, \(R_{i,t}\) resource states, and \(I_{i,t}\in\{0,1\}\) participation indicators.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A joint specification of statistical, model, systems, and participation variability affecting a federated optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A federated client-variability regime is the joint family \(\mathcal V=\{(f_i,M_i,(R_{i,t})_{t\ge0},(I_{i,t})_{t\ge0}):i\in\mathcal I\}\) together with quantitative bounds or probability laws governing variation across clients and time. Statistical variability concerns differences among \(f_i\) or their data laws; model variability concerns differences among \(M_i\) or client prediction maps; systems variability concerns compute, memory, energy, bandwidth, delay, or availability encoded by \(R_{i,t}\); participation variability concerns the joint law of \(I_{i,t}\). A regime is homogeneous along a coordinate only when the corresponding client objects are identical or satisfy the declared zero-variability condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A client-variability regime records the client objectives, model spaces, time-varying resource states, and participation indicators, together with mathematical bounds or laws describing their variation. This separates statistical heterogeneity from model, systems, and participation heterogeneity. The regime is not a single scalar unless a particular metric has been chosen; each coordinate requires its own declared comparison rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal V\) determines which client differences and participation processes are admitted by an analysis or algorithmic guarantee.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A parameterized regime may be summarized by a vector \((\zeta_{\mathrm{stat}},\zeta_{\mathrm{model}},\zeta_{\mathrm{sys}},\zeta_{\mathrm{part}})\) once each component metric is explicitly defined.
special_cases_latex: The fully homogeneous full-participation regime has identical local objectives and model spaces, constant resource states, and \(I_{i,t}=1\) for all \(i,t\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A guarantee stated for one variability coordinate need not cover variation in the other coordinates.
boundary_notes: The four coordinates may be statistically dependent.
A taxonomy does not itself impose bounded heterogeneity.

notation.meaning: client i's systems-resource state at time t
indicator that client i participates at time t

children.title: Client Data and Objective Heterogeneity
children.top_down_role: Differences among local data distributions, risks, and sample weights.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let client \(i\) have data law \(\mathcal D_i\), loss \(\ell_i(w;\xi)\), local risk \(f_i(w)=\mathbb E_{\xi\sim\mathcal D_i}[\ell_i(w;\xi)]\), and target weight \(p_i\). Let \(F(w)=\sum_i p_i f_i(w)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shared-parameter federated learning with heterogeneous client data laws, losses, risks, or objective weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Client distribution-objective heterogeneity is the failure of the weighted local optimization objects \((\mathcal D_i,\ell_i,f_i,p_i)\) to be identical across clients. Distribution heterogeneity occurs when \(\mathcal D_i
e\mathcal D_j\), including changes in covariate, label, conditional-label, or sample-size distributions. Objective heterogeneity occurs when \(f_i
e f_j\) because of different data laws, losses, regularizers, or task weights. At differentiability points, a quantitative gradient-dissimilarity measure is \(H(w)=\sum_i p_i\|
abla f_i(w)-
abla F(w)\|^2\); a bounded-dissimilarity regime on \(W_0\subseteq W\) requires \(H(w)\le\zeta^2\) for every \(w\in W_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Client distribution heterogeneity means clients have different data-generating laws. Objective heterogeneity means their local risk functions differ, potentially because of data, losses, regularizers, or task weights. A common smooth quantitative measure is the weighted squared deviation of local gradients from the global gradient. A bounded regime must state both its bound and the parameter region on which the bound holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regime \(H(w)\le\zeta^2\) for all \(w\in W_0\) quantifies smooth objective heterogeneity relative to the weighted global objective.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Since \(\nabla F(w)=\sum_i p_i\nabla f_i(w)\), \(H(w)\) is the weighted variance of client gradients at \(w\).
special_cases_latex: If \(f_i=f_j\) for all clients, then \(H(w)=0\) wherever the common objective is differentiable.
Different sample counts with sample-proportional weights alter \(p_i\) even when empirical distributions are otherwise similar.
immediate_consequences_latex: Equal objective values at one point do not imply zero gradient dissimilarity there.
boundary_notes: Distributional difference need not induce different risks for a particular loss class.
The displayed metric does not cover nonsmooth objectives without replacing gradients by an appropriate set-valued comparison.
review_flags: No federated heterogeneity source was supplied with an inspected exact locator.
knowledge_statements.title: Client distribution and objective heterogeneity
Statistical Heterogeneity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Statistical heterogeneity occurs when at least two clients have different data-generating distributions, regardless of how many samples each client holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let client \(i\) draw observations \(\xi\) from a probability distribution \(P_i\) on a common measurable sample space \((\Xi,\mathcal A)\). The federation has statistical heterogeneity when the family \(\{P_i\}_{i=1}^m\) is not constant, equivalently when there exist clients \(i\ne j\) and an event \(A\in\mathcal A\) such that \(P_i(A)\ne P_j(A)\). This may reflect differing covariate, label, conditional, or joint distributions, independently of unequal client sample counts.
assumptions_latex: All \(P_i\) are probability measures on the same measurable space \((\Xi,\mathcal A)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists i\ne j\) with \(P_i\ne P_j\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Client variability arising from unequal local data-generating distributions.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports this federated statistical-heterogeneity definition.
standard_field_rationale: unequal client data distributions are the standard mathematical meaning.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The definition is precise and matches the statistical-heterogeneity leaf, but no citation with an inspectable locator is supplied. The standard-field rationale is not enough to establish the exact federated taxonomy statement for review acceptance.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective Heterogeneity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective heterogeneity is gradient disagreement between client objectives and their weighted aggregate; its weighted squared norm gives a pointwise quantitative measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let differentiable client objectives \(F_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) have weights \(p_i\ge0\), \(\sum_i p_i=1\), and let \(F(w)=\sum_i p_iF_i(w)\). Their objective heterogeneity at \(w\) is measured by
\[H(w)=\sum_{i=1}^m p_i\|\nabla F_i(w)-\nabla F(w)\|^2.\]
The objectives are heterogeneous on a domain \(W\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) when \(H(w)>0\) for some \(w\in W\); a uniform heterogeneity bound is \(H(w)\le B^2\) for every \(w\in W\).
assumptions_latex: Each \(F_i\) is differentiable on \(W\subseteq\mathbb R^d\).
\(p_i\ge0\) and \(\sum_i p_i=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H(w)\ge0\), and \(H(w)=0\) exactly when every positive-weight client gradient equals \(\nabla F(w)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Client variability measured by disagreement among local objective gradients.
review_flags: Several inequivalent objective-heterogeneity measures exist, and no supporting locator was supplied.
The selected gradient-dissimilarity convention requires source confirmation.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the leaf, but objective heterogeneity has several inequivalent conventions. No source supports this particular weighted gradient-disagreement measure or the proposed uniform bound, so the selected mathematical version requires authoritative confirmation.

knowledge_statements.title: Client Sample-Weight Imbalance
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unequal client sample counts create unequal sample-proportional objective weights; the largest-to-smallest count ratio quantifies the imbalance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose client \(i\) holds \(n_i\ge1\) observations and its empirical objective is \(F_i(w)=n_i^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^{n_i}\ell(w;\xi_{ik})\). Sample-proportional aggregation assigns
\[p_i=\frac{n_i}{N},\qquad N=\sum_{j=1}^m n_j,\qquad F(w)=\sum_{i=1}^m p_iF_i(w).\]
Client sample-weight imbalance occurs when the weights are nonuniform, equivalently when some \(n_i\ne n_j\). It may be summarized by \(R=n_{\max}/n_{\min}\ge1\), with exact balance precisely when \(R=1\).
assumptions_latex: There are finitely many clients and every sample count satisfies \(n_i\ge1\).
The aggregate empirical risk weights every observation equally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Sample-weight imbalance holds exactly when \((p_1,\ldots,p_m)\ne(1/m,\ldots,1/m)\), equivalently \(R>1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unequal empirical-objective weights induced by unequal client sample sizes.

notation.meaning: number of observations at client i

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports this client-weight convention.
standard_field_rationale: sample-proportional empirical-risk weighting is standard, but other federation objectives may choose different weights.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the leaf and the equivalences are correct under sample-proportional aggregation. Because federated objectives may use weights not induced by sample counts, an authoritative source with a specific locator is required to support this exact convention and scope.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Client Distribution Shift
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cross-client distribution shift occurs when at least two clients have different data distributions on the same measurable sample space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Cross-client distribution shift is the condition
\[
\exists i\ne j:\ P_i\ne P_j,
\]
equivalently, there exists \(A\in\mathcal A\) with \(P_i(A)\ne P_j(A)\). For a common loss, the induced objectives are \(F_i(x)=\int_{\mathcal Z}\ell(x;z)\,dP_i(z)\). Distribution shift need not imply \(F_i\ne F_j\), because distinct measures can yield identical expectations for the chosen loss class; conversely, the condition concerns the data-generating measures themselves.
assumptions_latex: Clients are indexed by \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and client \(i\) draws data from a probability measure \(P_i\) on a common measurable space \((\mathcal Z,\mathcal A)\).
A common measurable loss \(\ell:X\times\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R\) induces \(F_i(x)=\mathbb E_{Z\sim P_i}[\ell(x;Z)]\) whenever the expectation exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cross-client distribution shift holds exactly when \(P_i\ne P_j\) for some clients \(i,j\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributional, rather than merely objective-value, heterogeneity on a shared sample space.

notation.meaning: Expected local objective induced by client i

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The distributional condition is mathematically standard and fits the leaf, but no inspectable citation supports this federated-learning usage. The parameter domain X is also not introduced as a set.

children.title: Systems Heterogeneity
children.top_down_role: Differences in compute, memory, energy, bandwidth, and availability.

knowledge_statements.title: Systems Heterogeneity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Systems heterogeneity means that clients differ over time in compute, memory, energy, communication capacity, latency, or availability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
r_i(t)=(c_i(t),m_i(t),e_i(t),b_i(t),a_i(t))\in\mathcal R
\]
record client \(i\)'s compute capacity, memory, energy budget, bandwidth or latency characteristics, and availability at time \(t\). The federation has systems heterogeneity on a relevant time set \(T\) when
\[
\exists i\ne j,\ 
exists t\in T:\ r_i(t)\ne r_j(t).
\]
The definition permits deterministic, stochastic, and time-varying profiles and does not require the clients' data distributions or objectives to differ.
assumptions_latex: At time \(t\), client \(i\) has a resource-and-availability profile \(r_i(t)\) in a common profile space \(\mathcal R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Systems heterogeneity holds when \(r_i(t)\ne r_j(t)\) for some clients and relevant time.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Time-dependent device and communication variability, independent of statistical data differences.

notation.meaning: Compute, memory, energy, communication, and availability profile of client i

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the systems-heterogeneity container, but it has no citation. In the displayed condition, the second existential appears as plain 'exists' rather than \exists and therefore does not express the intended quantified condition correctly.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For client \(i\) and round \(t\), let \(R_{i,t}=(c_{i,t},m_{i,t},e_{i,t},b_{i,t},\delta_{i,t},a_{i,t})\) encode compute rate, memory, energy budget, bandwidth, communication delay, and availability.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Time-varying operational heterogeneity of federated clients, distinct from their data distributions and objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Systems heterogeneity is cross-client or temporal nonidentity of the resource processes \(\{R_{i,t}\}\). Given a task requiring \(u_{i,t}\) compute operations, \(s_{i,t}\) memory, \(v_{i,t}\) energy, and \(q_{i,t}\) communicated bits, client \(i\) is operationally feasible at round \(t\) only if \(a_{i,t}=1\), \(s_{i,t}\le m_{i,t}\), \(v_{i,t}\le e_{i,t}\), and its compute and communication complete within the declared deadline, for example \(u_{i,t}/c_{i,t}+q_{i,t}/b_{i,t}+\delta_{i,t}\le D_t\). A systems-heterogeneity regime specifies the admissible set or joint law of these resource vectors rather than assuming identical clients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Systems heterogeneity is variation across clients or time in computation, memory, energy, bandwidth, latency, and availability. A local task is feasible only when the client is available, its memory and energy requirements fit its budgets, and its compute-plus-communication time meets the declared deadline. A rigorous regime specifies admissible resource vectors or their probability law; merely saying that devices are different is not a mathematical condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible participant set at round \(t\) consists of clients whose resource vector satisfies every declared task constraint.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A straggler model may encode systems heterogeneity through random completion times \(T_{i,t}\), with participation accepted only when \(T_{i,t}\le D_t\).
special_cases_latex: Homogeneous synchronous clients have identical deterministic \(R_{i,t}=R\) and a common deadline.
immediate_consequences_latex: Client selection based on completion feasibility can correlate participation with device type or data distribution.
boundary_notes: Systems heterogeneity does not mean statistical heterogeneity, although the two may be correlated.
The displayed latency model is additive and excludes communication-computation overlap.

notation.meaning: systems-resource vector of client i at round t

review_flags: No inspected source locator supports this resource-vector formalization.

children.title: Model Heterogeneity
children.top_down_role: Federation across distinct architectures or parameterizations.

knowledge_statements.title: Model Heterogeneity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Model heterogeneity occurs when clients use distinct architectures or parameter spaces but retain a defined shared coordination or prediction interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A federation is model-heterogeneous when its clients use local model classes \(\mathcal H_i=\{h_{i,\theta}:\theta\in\Theta_i\}\) for which
\[
\exists i\ne j:\ (\Theta_i,\mathcal H_i)\ne(
\Theta_j,\mathcal H_j),
\]
while a common coordination interface remains available. Such an interface may be a variable \(z\in Z\) with client realizations \(D_i(z)\in\Theta_i\), a shared representation, or comparable predictions in \(\mathcal Y\). Direct coordinatewise parameter averaging is defined only when compatible embeddings into a common vector space have been specified.
assumptions_latex: Client \(i\) optimizes parameters \(\theta_i\in\Theta_i\) and produces outputs in a common prediction space \(\mathcal Y\).
Federated coordination is expressed through a common variable \(z\in Z\) and client-specific maps \(D_i:Z\to\Theta_i\), or through an equivalent shared prediction-level constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Model heterogeneity holds when the local model classes or parameterizations are not all identical while a common coordination interface remains defined.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the model-heterogeneity leaf, but the proposed coordination-interface formulation is not source-supported. The model classes h_{i,\theta} are also not assigned a common input domain.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let client \(i\) use parameter space \(\Theta_i\), predictor \(h_i:\Theta_i\times\mathcal X_i\to\mathcal Y_i\), and local risk \(f_i:\Theta_i\to\mathbb R\). Let \(Z\) be a shared representation or coordination space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Federated optimization across clients whose architectures, parameter dimensions, or parameterizations need not coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A federation is model-heterogeneous when there exist clients \(i,j\) for which the model classes or parameterizations differ, so \(\Theta_i\ne\Theta_j\), \(h_i(\Theta_i)\ne h_j(\Theta_j)\), or no canonical coordinatewise averaging map between their parameters exists. A model-heterogeneous optimization problem specifies client parameters \(\theta_i\in\Theta_i\), local risks \(f_i(\theta_i)\), maps \(E_i:\Theta_i\to Z\) into a common coordination space, and a coupling functional \(\Psi((E_i\theta_i)_i)\), and minimizes \(\sum_i p_i f_i(\theta_i)+\lambda\Psi((E_i\theta_i)_i)\). The maps and coupling identify what information is shared despite architectural differences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Model heterogeneity occurs when clients use different model classes, architectures, dimensions, or parameterizations, so direct coordinatewise parameter averaging is undefined or semantically invalid. A formal heterogeneous-model federation gives every client its own parameter space and risk, maps client models into a common coordination space, and couples them there through a declared functional. The coupling may align predictions, representations, prototypes, or another shared object.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The shared optimization object is \(\min_{\theta_i\in\Theta_i}\sum_i p_if_i(\theta_i)+\lambda\Psi((E_i\theta_i)_i)\), with \(E_i\) and \(\Psi\) defining interoperability.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Prediction-level coupling is obtained when \(E_i\theta_i\) denotes client predictions on a common reference input set.
special_cases_latex: If all \(\Theta_i=\mathbb R^d\), all architectures agree, and \(E_i\) is the identity, the formulation reduces to a parameter-homogeneous coupled model.
immediate_consequences_latex: Parameter averaging is not intrinsically defined when client parameter dimensions differ.
boundary_notes: Different parameter values within one common architecture are not model heterogeneity.
Model heterogeneity is distinct from different client data distributions.
